name: Opportunity Rover
purpose: Search rocks and soil for clues about past water activity on Mars.
story: Opportunity was built to work for just 90 Martian days. It kept exploring for almost 15 years.
The rover crossed dusty plains, examined rocks, and explored craters. Its instruments found evidence that liquid water had once changed parts of Mars.

A planet-wide dust storm in 2018 blocked sunlight from reaching its solar panels. Opportunity sent its last signal on June 10, 2018. After many attempts to contact it, NASA declared the mission complete in February 2019.
legacy: Opportunity travelled about 45.16 kilometres (28.06 miles) and helped show that ancient Mars had environments where liquid water was present. It did not discover life. Whether life ever existed there remains an open question.

evidence.label: Confirmed finding
evidence.text: Opportunity found geological evidence of ancient environments where liquid water was present.

evidence.label: Scientific interpretation
evidence.text: Some ancient Martian environments may once have been capable of supporting microbial life. This is an interpretation of environmental evidence, not a discovery of life.

evidence.label: Still unknown
evidence.text: Did life ever exist on Mars? Opportunity did not answer this question.

openQuestion.prompt: Mars once had water. What would you search for next?
evidenceOptions: A microscope to study tiny textures
A drill to collect protected rock samples
A camera to map layers in the rocks
A chemistry instrument to identify minerals

name: Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle
date: First driven on the Moon: July 31, 1971
status: Inactive · left on the lunar surface after each mission
purpose: Carry astronauts, tools and samples farther across the lunar surface than they could walk.
story: Imagine exploring the Moon in a small electric car. The Lunar Roving Vehicle made that possible for Apollo astronauts.
The rover folded up for the journey inside the Lunar Module. On the Moon, astronauts unfolded it, powered it up and drove across the surface to explore places farther from their landing site.
Three Lunar Roving Vehicles were used: one each on Apollo 15, Apollo 16 and Apollo 17. They were not designed to return to Earth. They remain where the missions left them.
legacy: The rover extended the distance astronauts could travel while collecting lunar samples and conducting science. The three vehicles are historic hardware still resting on the Moon.

evidence.label: Confirmed finding
evidence.text: Three Lunar Roving Vehicles were driven on the Moon during Apollo 15, 16 and 17.
evidence.source: NASA NSSDC Lunar Roving Vehicle overview

evidence.label: Scientific interpretation
evidence.text: By allowing crews to travel farther, the rover increased the range of terrain and geological samples astronauts could investigate.

evidence.label: Still unknown
evidence.text: How will decades of lunar dust, temperature changes and radiation affect the rover materials over very long periods?
evidence.source: Future investigation question; not a settled NASA finding

name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
status: Inactive · mission ended January 25, 2024; rotor-blade damage prevents flight
purpose: Demonstrate the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
story: Ingenuity was a tiny helicopter that travelled to Mars attached beneath the Perseverance rover.
Flying on Mars was a huge challenge. Its atmosphere is very thin, so its rotor blades had to spin very fast. On April 19, 2021, Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
It was designed for up to five flights. It completed 72. During its final flight on January 18, 2024, one or more rotor blades were damaged. NASA announced the end of the mission on January 25, 2024.
legacy: Ingenuity proved that powered flight is possible on another planet. Its flights also showed how aerial scouts could help future missions explore difficult terrain.

evidence.label: Confirmed finding
evidence.text: Ingenuity completed 72 flights on Mars, beginning with its first powered, controlled flight on April 19, 2021.

evidence.label: Scientific interpretation
evidence.text: Aerial vehicles could help future missions scout routes and inspect terrain that is difficult for rovers to reach.

evidence.label: Still unknown
evidence.text: What new science could a larger, more capable future Mars rotorcraft investigate?

openQuestion.prompt: What should the next flying explorer on Mars investigate?
